5511ee44af: Twinkle Twinkle's melody only uses 1 to 6: the right thumb sits on C, finger 5 covers G, and finger 5 reaches over for the sixth note, A.

ebd32fa53b: For songs with a wider range, move your hand on long notes or rests, or use Lesson 3's thumb-unders and crossings. Once you've settled the fingering, use the same one every time.
3910c91d59: Pencilling finger numbers onto the numbered notation is a good pop piano habit. It looks like a chore the first time; by the tenth, your fingers remember on their own.

1578a53e88: All three notes pressed together, left-hand fingering 5 3 1. Careful not to play louder than the right-hand melody.
f0e55662f5: The original materials' teaching order: get the left hand comfortable with fifths first, then add right-hand octave fingering. Fifths are the most common left-hand foundation in pop piano.

0a97101701: Slow soul: the most common rhythm in today's pop
be85c58b2f: Goes up and holds, leaving room for the melody
ca4eec7fe9: Up and back down, flowing eighth notes
9756813a8a: The fifth swings back and forth like a pendulum
d7b7b964f1: You can mix the four patterns: use (1) in the verse to leave space, and switch to (2) or (4) in the chorus to lift the mood.
62d1c16952: Four slow soul accompaniments: listen first, then play along
6fea4e13a0: Which note is L2 in a G chord?
dc6a96d2ab: L2 is the fifth: a G chord is G B D, and the fifth is D.
e1600ed2ee: To keep the verse quiet and leave room for the melody, which pattern fits best?
4107ae97e1: (1) goes up and holds for two beats, with the fewest notes, so it sets off the melody best.
c0e76904be: Ten-minute break: tap out 5 3 2 1 on the table with your left hand
be499ffdf5: Strong, weak, weak: four accompaniments in triple time
ea3ca9a771: Listen for the time signature and tempo, then choose the left hand
80000b836b: Use an accompaniment with fewer notes in the verse so the voice is clear; switch to one with more notes and a wider range in the chorus and the mood rises naturally. Lesson 7 practises switching between 4 beats and 8 beats.
a06406ddb5: The more notes in the accompaniment, the better it sounds
1931b16231: MythAn accompaniment that's too full drowns the melody and voice; leaving space is a skill too.
96556b4272: When the chord changes, the accompaniment's finger positions stay the same
b586c5531f: FactThe whole hand shifts to the new root and you play the same finger-position pattern.
f23f37d08e: Songs in triple time are always slow
52c98b53d6: MythTime signature has nothing to do with tempo; fast waltzes are common too.
f6ebd8466e: The left-hand accompaniment should be quieter than the right hand
7f3e54bd60: FactThe melody is the star and the accompaniment the stage; a lighter left hand lets the melody float above.
502e6d8600: You can only use the pedal once you've learned everything else
d9fecf59a8: MythBroken chords sound best with the sustain pedal; just remember to change the pedal with each chord.
f1214edae0: A song can only use one accompaniment
0614c4f757: MythUsing different accompaniments for the verse and chorus is common in pop piano.
